Title: On the Slopes of Yr Wyddfa (Snowdon) - Eryri
Summary:
Join us for a weekend in the
Nant Gwynant
area, staying in a
recently renovated mountain bunkhouse
beneath the southern slopes of
Yr Wyddfa (Snowdon)
.
Nant Gwynant is one of the main gateways into southern Eryri (Snowdonia). The
Watkin Path starts directly outside the front door
, while Beddgelert, the Glaslyn valley and the lakes of Nant Gwynant are all within easy reach. The area combines mountains, lakes, rivers, woodland and the remains of Eryri's industrial past, making it an excellent base for a walking weekend.
One of the biggest advantages of staying here is that
all walks will start directly from the bunkhouse
, allowing us to leave the cars behind for the weekend and explore the area on foot.
We'll arrive on Friday evening, with our traditional OutdoorLads buffet to start the weekend. Breakfasts are included on both mornings, along with a shared evening meal on Saturday.
Walking
The walks offered will depend on the leaders available for the weekend.
If sufficient Mountain Walk Leaders are available, we hope to offer mountain walks on both days. Possible routes include
Yr Wyddfa (Snowdon)
via the Watkin Path and
Cnicht
.
If mountain leadership isn't available, we'll instead make use of the extensive network of paths around Nant Gwynant, Beddgelert and the Glaslyn valley. These lower-level routes still provide access to some of the best scenery in Eryri without venturing onto the higher mountains.
Final walk details will be confirmed once the event attendance is known.
The Bunkhouse
Our base for the weekend is a traditional stone mountain bunkhouse that has recently undergone a major refurbishment. It combines modern facilities with the character of a historic mountain property, creating an excellent base for exploring this part of Eryri.
Facilities include comfortable bunk rooms, a well-equipped kitchen, dining area, sitting room with a wood-burning stove, drying room and modern shower facilities. With the Watkin Path passing the front door, we can simply step outside and start walking.
The Area
The bunkhouse is ideally located for exploring the Nant Gwynant area. Nearby are the
Watkin waterfalls
,
Llyn Dinas
,
Llyn Gwynant
,
Cwm Llan
and the
Glaslyn
river, while
Beddgelert
can be reached on foot along public footpaths.
The surrounding area includes some of Eryri's best-known mountains, including
Yr Wyddfa (Snowdon)
,
Cnicht
,
Moel Hebog
and the
Nantlle Ridge
, alongside quieter valleys and woodland for lower-level walks.
Parking
Parking at the bunkhouse is available for around eight vehicles. The nearest public parking is in Beddgelert, approximately 3.5 miles away. Car sharing may therefore be required for this event. If you can offer lifts, or would like one, please indicate this by messaging  the event leader once you have booked, so we can coordinate transport before the weekend. We will get everyone there somehow!
Staying on Sunday Night
The event officially finishes on Sunday afternoon. However, you're welcome to stay for a third night on Sunday at no additional cost if you'd like to make more of the weekend and reduce the amount of travelling.
If you choose to stay, there will usually be enough food available for breakfast on Monday morning, but an evening meal on Sunday is not included. You'll therefore need to provide your own meal, either by cooking at the bunkhouse or eating out locally.
Please let the leader know nearer the time if you intend to stay on Sunday night. A walk will still be offered on the Sunday before the event finishes.

This event is not suitable for dogs.

All images are event leaders own with permission given to OutdoorLads for use and reuse

Title: Where the Crane meets planes. Walk, nature & picnic at LHR
Summary:
I've been visiting the viewing area by Myrtle Avenue, by the landing lights for years, to watch the planes landing at Heathrow and often thought it would be great to get an ODL group together for a picnic and to enjoy the big jets. I know there are a lot of guys like me who like aviation, or maybe you fancy doing something a bit different. Add to that a flat, easy walk along the River Crane from Twickenham, and I think its a fun little day out.
There are two options: a walk and picnic or just the picnic.
The Walk
Join me on this easy flat linear walk from Twickenham station following the River Crane as it meanders to Heathrow Airport. There's an optional walk around a small nature reserve by Crane Park.
The walk route map can be viewed in OS Maps
here
.
Points of interest
River Crane
The River Crane, a tributary of the River Thames, runs 8.5 miles (13.6 km). It forms the lower course of Yeading Brook. It adjoins or passes through three London boroughs: Hillingdon, Hounslow and Richmond upon Thames.
Crane Park & Shot Tower
Crane Park is a 30 hectare public park next to the River Crane. The Hounslow Gunpowder Works opened in the late 1760s in what is now the western end of the park. Crane Park Island was created to provide a mill pond for the water to drive the machinery. There were many explosions and the Shot Tower is now thought to have been a windmill for recirculating water to power the mills, rather than a shot tower for making lead shot.
The licence to manufacture gunpowder was withdrawn in 1927, and part of the site was sold to Twickenham Council, which turned it into Crane Park. This opened in 1935. The Shot Tower (now officially the Brick Tower) is a Grade II listed building.
Crane Park Island Nature Reserve
There is a short circular walk of the reserve for those who wish to visit.
Heathrow Airport
The airport was opened on 25 March 1946 as London Airport; taking on the role of the UKs main International Airport from Croydon. It was renamed Heathrow Airport in September 1966. The airport's Central Terminal Area (CTA) was designed by Sir Frederick Gibberd, who set out the terminals and central-area buildings, including the control tower and the multi-faith Chapel of St George's.
The airport consists of Terminals 2, 3, 4 & 5 and handles 1,300 flight movements daily and connects passengers to around 230 direct destinations across 85 countries, served by over 80 airlines.
The Picnic
The plan is to have a picnic at the end of the walk at the viewing area known as Myrtle Avenue. What 3 words:
///yarn.rested.stack
We should be able to see aircraft landing on runway 27L before they switch to 27R at 15.00. However the runway alteration programme can change depending on the wind direction, but hopefully we'll get some take off's or landings.
You can of course just come for the picnic. We will aim to be at the viewing area by 13.30 or thereabouts.
If you only wish to attend the picnic, please sign up as usual but add in the comments below that you are  only attending the picnic.
You might want to bring a blanket, rug or something to sit on as the ground is dry and dusty. Bring food and drink with you or the BP petrol station 2 mins walk is well stocked. There is also a toilet here.
New Members
New members are very welcome. Please message me if you have any questions or concerns before the day.
All Images were taken by Neil Prior & permission given to OutdoorLads for re-use.
Difficulty & Distance: 11km/7 miles on easy, flat gravel and tarmac paths

Title: Llanberis: heritage and natural beauty
Summary:
The landscape of Llanberis in the heart of Eryri is like nowhere else. The town sits at the junction of two lakes Llyn Padarn and Llyn Peris and lies at the foot of Yr Wyddfa the highest mountain in England and Wales.
In the past is was a place where hundreds of men exported thousands of tons of slate through the ports of Caernarfon and Bangor. Nowadays it is a centre for outdoor activities of all sorts, and the starting point of two steam powered railways, the most famous being the one that ascends Yr Wyddfa.
The area may carry the scars of two centuries of slate quarrying but it still provides attractive foregrounds for some of the finest and most famous views. Quite often, the best views of mountains are not from the summits, nor the valleys, but from halfway above on the opposite side as is the case with this walk.
This event is more of a multi facetted day out as well as a good walk. Our journey combines the stark and remarkable slate workings of the Dinorwig quarries, views of the lakes and mountains, a castle visit and a small museum.
We will start with a look at the remains of Castle Dolbadarn (free entry) - one of the original Welsh castles built by Llewyn ap Iowerth to defend the are from the marauding Anglo Saxons.
Then there's a pretty steep 1 mile uphill incline passing the famous Anglesey Barracks, a ruined row of miners cottages seen on many postcards and biscuit tins.
The climb rewards us with a truly superb viewpoint. After this we will go on to see some of the shear rock faces and extraordinary mine workings which are on a vast scale and popular with daring climbers.
The route then drops back down through the forest above Llyn Peris and gives us the opportunity for a quick visit into a museum which was a hospital to treat wounded quarry workers and contains exhibits of historical medical equipment and practices – a fascinating glimpse into the past. (free entry)
Dogs
are welcome to join us on this event but please note the following:
This route may pass through areas with livestock.  Your dog needs to be well behaved and be on a lead at times. It must not affect other member's enjoyment of the event.  There may be stiles to carry your dog across. Your dog needs to have the stamina to keep up with the group.

Title: SE500: The White Horse of Uffington
Summary:
This walk has been conceived, written & illustrated by
Frankie Bruce
, who has pioneered the idea of challenging hill walks in the relatively flat south-east of England for OutdoorLads. Our grateful thanks to Frankie for preparing the event for us.
-----------------------------------------------------------------
This is a spectacular walk taking in the very best of the White Horse hills, on mostly good tracks. The walk takes in ancient history as well as manor houses and passes race horse gallops. Do have a look at Frankie's photos and the special video he has prepared for this walk below.
This walk is part of the SE500 series, covering a slightly longer distance and more ascent than your average hill walk. In total, over 500 metres of ascent are covered, which should help you burn off an average of 2100 calories.
The walk begins with a circle of Woolstone Wells valley, and a steep ascent onto the
Dragon’s Hill
. This is a mound which is bare on top, exposing the chalk, as no grass will grow here. Legend has it this is because the blood of a dragon was spilled here.
We then circle the
White Horse of Uffington
to gain the very best views of this site. This is a huge chalk figure of a horse in the hillside, dating from the Bronze Age around 4000 years ago. It is 114 metres long – a colossal and well-known site. It is thought it was of importance to the ancient Celts. Another rumour was that the horse was created by King Alfred in celebration of a battle victory, but it has actually been dated as much older than that.
There is evidence of other fortifications in the smaller humps nearby, which date from the Iron Age. Our route climbs onto
Uffington Castle
with its fortification mounds, itself an Iron Age hill fort which was built on top of the Bronze Age one.
Descending from the fort, the route crosses ancient ditches below Woolstone Down Gallops, a training ground for the finest race horses. The route continues over gently rolling hills and fields to Weathercock Hill to Ashdown Park (National Trust). The house was built by Lord William of Craven in the 1660s. We follow paths through the woods with a good view of the house.
We then turn north and head up over Odstone Down and continue for two miles over rolling downs. Where the track turns left, look across the field to
Wayland's Smithy
, an atmospheric neolithic warrior’s long barrow burial ground. This is about 5500 years old! Wayland or Wolund was named after a god in Norse mythology.
The route descends to
Ashbury village
, with its quaint thatched cottages, pub, village shop and café and manor house. There may be an opportunity for an afternoon break stop here. We then ascend most of the way up Odstone Hill with good views north west.
The ornate Compton Beauchamp House, a Baroque style stately home, was originally a moated manor house built by Sir Thomas Fettiplace in 1507. Nearly there! The return rises above Woolstone Village up the hill to start, using the path in the access land to the left of the road.

1. White Horse Hill Trig Point 2.1K 140m completed; 18.4K 372m to go
2. Weathercock Hill 7.6K 209m / 12.9K 303m

4. Odstone Hill  15.6K 368m / 4.9K 144m

Title: 'A Haunt of Ancient Peace' - Parham in Autumn
Summary:
"Nothing at Parham is superfluous, nothing unloved. It is a house of magic." (Simon Jenkins,
England's Thousand Best Houses
)
"An English house - gray twilight pour'd / On dewy pastures, dewy trees, / Softer than sleep - all things in order stored, / A haunt of ancient peace." (Tennyson,
The Palace of Art
)
Simon Jenkins considers Parham House to be not just among England's thousand best, or even among its hundred best. He considers it to be among its twenty best, on a par with Chatsworth, Blenheim and Hardwick Hall. To me it is superior to those, eschewing military pomp and showy boastfulness; 'a haunt of ancient peace' indeed. Built in 1577 before the era of Elizabethan 'prodigy houses' like Hardwick, it is straightforward and sober in design, but the interiors are Elizabethan and Jacobean at their finest. Sunday 11 October will be the last time it opens in 2026, and we'll
walk
three and a half picturesque downland miles to get there from Amberley Station.
The chief points of interest at
Parham House
and Park are:
The deer park, which is a chase of big trees and bracken with the bare South Downs behind as a dramatic backdrop.
A classic Elizabethan E-shaped plan, although the east wing has been much altered and was restored to its Tudor design in the twentieth century.
The Great Hall with bay windows from floor to ceiling, flooding the heraldry and portraits with light.
A picture collection of Tudor royalty and statesmen, including the famous portrait of the doomed Henry, Prince of Wales being pursued by winged Time from 1611.
The Saloon, designed and decorated in 1790, so bringing the Georgian era to the building.
The Green Room, dedicated to Sir Joseph Banks, explorer and president of The Royal Society. His portrait is by Joshua Reynolds and there are paintings of exotic animals by George Stubbs.
The Long Gallery, which stretches the length of the South Front and was designed for indoor exercise. The vista down the gallery is superb.
The gardens are seven acres of Pleasure Grounds, laid out in the 18th century, with a lake, a brick and turf maze and many specimen trees.
The Walled Garden contains romantic wide herbaceous borders, a rose garden, a cut flower garden, a vegetable garden, and an orchard. The Greenhouse has a fine display of pelargoniums.
The finest collection of historic needlework outside of London.
Fresh floral arrangements in every room for the duration of the season.
If we set off from Amberley at 11.00, we should reach Parham by 12.20. The gardens will be open then, so we can explore those and have lunch. The house opens at 14.00.
The cost of entrance to the house and gardens is £15.88 with Gift Aid or £14.43 without it. Parham is privately owned, so unfortunately National Trust or English Heritage memberships won't be of use. Historic Houses members gain free admission, however, and RHS members can gain free admission to the gardens, and the house for an extra £4.

Title: Bouldering MANCHESTER - Beginners welcome
Summary:
Join OutdoorLads For An Evening of INDOOR BOULDERING in Manchester!
This event is intended as a safe space for the LGBTQ+ community; everyone will be warmly welcomed
Bouldering is a form of climbing that focuses on shorter "problems" emphasising technique, balance, body positioning, and sometimes power, rather than long, high routes. Without the need for ropes, harnesses, and belaying, bouldering is an accessible activity for newcomers and is often considered the "purest" form of climbing.
Bouldering offers a wide range of benefits, including:
Physical:
Improved strength, tone, balance, power, and coordination.
Mental:
Enhanced problem-solving, focus, concentration, and body awareness.
Emotional:
Relaxation, a sense of achievement, and a feeling of mind-body connection.
Bouldering is also a fantastic way to meet new people and build lasting friendships, as it's an inherently social sport where climbers share tips and strategies to conquer the routes.
New to Bouldering?
If you're new to bouldering, it is recommended that you have a guided session from the event leader to learn the basics of safe bouldering. The leader can then introduce you to the rest of the group where you can refine your newly learnt skills in a social environment.
Experienced Boulderer?
If you’re new to climbing with ODL, the leader will help to introduce you to the rest of the group so you can explore the centre together.
You are responsible for your own safety and actions while bouldering. Please use your own judgement when accepting advice from OutdoorLads Volunteers or other experienced climbers, regardless of your bouldering experience.
Ready to boulder?
You will need to sign up on the ODL event page. We would ask you to do this each time so that the leader has access to important information
If you are not already registered with Rock Over Climbing, please do so
here
to save time when you arrive. You only need to do this once.
When you arrive at the centre you will need to pay for entry and hire climbing shoes if you don't own a pair. ODL members benefit from the concessionary rate so please mention this when paying.
Get bouldering! You’ll find most of the group already bouldering so feel free to join them. If you’re new to bouldering with ODL, the leader will be looking out for you so if you spot them, please go speak with them first.
Any questions?
If you have any questions, please contact the leader directly.
Photos : Copyright granted to OutdoorLads by
Sieh
and joenellist.
Difficulty & Distance: Suitable for all abilities. If you're new to bouldering, just let the event leader know and we'll get you started!

Title: Indoor Climbing MANCHESTER - Beginners welcome!
Summary:
This event is intended as a safe space for the LGBTQ+ community; everyone will be warmly welcomed
Join us for an evening of climbing in one of the UK's top climbing centres. Whether you are new to climbing or a seasoned climber, this centre offers something for everyone with a huge selection of routes including top rope, lead and auto belay.
Prefer to boulder? That's well catered for as well, with an extensive modern bouldering area ensuring there is plenty to keep you busy, or you can swap between climbing and bouldering on the same night.
Climbing is the main focus of the event, but this is also a great chance to meet other members and build lasting friendships. Many Outdoor Lads members join through climbing, so if you're new to the group and want to know more, come along and chat over a cuppa during the tea and cake break.
What to expect on your first climb with us?
If you are an experienced climber and have passed the centre's proficiency test, we'll pair you up with a climbing buddy and you'll be out exploring the centre in no time.
If you have never climbed before or think you could do with a refresher, we offer supervised climbing sessions with one of our leaders, subject to availability. That session will focus on introducing you to climbing, making sure you get plenty of time on the wall whilst also showing you how to belay safely. Due to the centre's rules, we are limited in the number of climbers the leader is able to supervise in each session so if you think you may need a supervised session,
please contact the leader before signing up to make sure there is enough space.
As a general guide, if you answer "no" to any of the following questions, you should opt for a supervised session:
Can you fit a climbing harness correctly?
Can you tie into a rope using the correct knots?
Can you belay and lower down another climber correctly and confidently?
After a few supervised sessions, you should be ready to complete the centre's proficiency test and once that has been passed, you'll be able to climb with the rest of the group.
Everything else you need to know
You will need to register with Big Depot before your first visit to the centre but you only need to do this once. If you are an experienced climber, you can save time and do this online
here
, selecting the 18+ unsupervised option. This also applies if you just want to boulder, just select the relevant options during the registration. If you are a beginner and require a supervised session, the leader will help register you when you are at the centre.

Difficulty & Distance: There is a range of routes of varying difficulty, but there should be something to suit everybody

Title: Baslow to Rowsley - DVH Way Section 3
Summary:
The Derwent Valley Trust
was set up in 1996 to promote the history, arts, wildlife and leisure opportunities that surround the river Derwent along its 55 mile course through Derbyshire.
The Derwent Valley Heritage Way
takes us from Ladybower Reservoir in the Peak District National Park to its end at Derwent Mouth where it flows into the River Trent near Shardlow. The Duke of Devonshire opened the walk at Chatsworth House in 2003.
The route takes us through the Chatsworth estate, Derbyshire dales, towns, villages, canals and many points of interests through the
Derwent Valley Mills World Heritage Site
. There are plenty of pubs and tea shops for refreshments along the way. The route follows the riverside path through Derby City and continues southeastwards to the historic inland port of Shardlow. Journey’s end is at Derwent Mouth where the Derwent flows into the River Trent.
The route is divided into eight sections of between  ~13 km (8 miles) and ~17 km (10.5 miles), each with a clear public transport solution. All, except the first section, are linear routes. We park at the end, travel to the start, and walk back to our cars. Sections 5, 6, 7 are brilliantly served by the East Midlands Railway Derwent Valley Line
(Derby–Matlock, hourly), which runs almost parallel to the trail the whole way. For sections (2, 3, 4 and 8), we use local buses.
Each section is a walk in itself. Join one or more, as you wish, or walk all eight sections to complete the whole route through Derbyshire. Please ask other attendees for a lift if you need one.
Section 3 - Baslow to Rowsley ~14 km (8.7 miles) Total ascent 199 m (653 ft)
The highlight of this section of the Way is the impressive
Chatsworth Estate
, with its house set in an extensive deer park landscaped by Lancelot (Capability) Brown. The 4th Duke of Devonshire (1720-64) had a channel cut across an S-bend upstream of the House to straighten the river and deal with intermittent flooding.
The route takes us through the stable yard, where refreshments are available, then we climb up to the top of the Cascade and across to the hunting lodge from where there are great views across the estate. The Emperor Fountain, which sends up a 88 m (290 feet) jet of water, is one of the park’s striking features.
Edensor village originally straggled across the valley so the 4th Duke removed a mill and some cottages to make room for the new 'one arch' bridge. In the 19th century, the 6th Duke and Joseph Paxton had the rest of Edensor demolished and rebuilt where it is today. Each house is a different design. The single house opposite the Edensor gates was spared because it was occupied by an old man at the time and the Duke did not want to disturb him.
The enlarged 14th century church of St Peter contains, among others features, a memorial to Paxton, the tomb of two sons of Bess of Hardwick, everlasting memorial flowers sent by Queen Victoria, and the grave of Kathleen Kennedy, sister of President John F Kennedy, who died in an air crash in 1948.
As the route winds through the estate south to Rowsley, there are close views of the Derwent.
At the end of this section we visit Caudwell’s Mill, a 19th-century grade II listed roller flour mill with pre-1914 machinery powered by two water turbines. There are several craft outlets and a shop on site selling different types of flour.

Title: SE500 Cromer (with easier option)
Summary:
This walk consists of 2 parts:
Part 1 - Moderate walk Cromer to Sheringham
- 9.1K (6 miles) then get the train back.
Part 2 -(optional) SE500 - walk back to Cromer via a different route
- total 20.6K (13 miles) and 500m ascent.
Everyone
will walk
Part 1
first, then you can choose whether to continue with
Part 2
or get the train back to Cromer.
You are most welcome to join this beautiful walk taking in sweeping panoramas of the Norfolk coast, the highest point in the county, as well as the Cromer Ridge and woodlands. New members are welcome and will find this a friendly, small group walk which provides a great introduction to Outdoorlads.
Cromer
is known as the gem of the Norfolk Coast. It’s Victorian Pier and Pavilion Theatre are prominent landmarks. Brightly painted beach huts line the promenade, whilst poppies adorn the hilltops beside the coast. After taking in the view from the coastal hill, we follow paths inland to Incleborough Hill.
Incleborough Hill
is a common west of Cromer, rising 79 metres above sea level, has excellent views across the landscape and out to sea. Glaciers from Norway melted at the end of an Ice Age, depositing gravel here which made the hill. Today, buzzards, honey buzzards, sparrowhawks, and kestrels can be spotted.
Next, we top
Beacon Hill
, the county top (highest point) in Norfolk at 105m. It is known as a Roman Camp by locals. Scenic panoramas of the coastline can be seen from here. Nightjar birds can sometimes be spotted. This area forms the Cromer Ridge.
The
Cromer Ridge
was used to defend the coast from invasion over the centuries. Beacon fires were lit on the ridge to signal to other villages along the coast that invaders were coming. These were used since Roman times then later to warn of the Spanish Armada under Elizabeth I. In places on the ridge there is evidence of World War Two: earthworks, practice trenches, weapons pits, and gun placements.
Iron smelting pits dating from Saxon times were found by archaeologists here. Apparently, the site was very good for blowing, using the coastal air. Returning to the coast,
Beeston Bump
provides a good view heading towards Sheringham. There was a listening station here to detect U-Boat signals during World War Two.
We follow the coastal path to the High Street where we will stop for lunch.
You can choose
here whether to continue with
Part 2
or get the train back to Cromer.
Sheringham to Cromer trains run hourly at roughly XX45 minutes past the hour and take 8 minutes, single fare £4.10.
After lunch,
Part 2
follows a different route back to Cromer, which is inland and goes over more of the Cromer Ridge, with some steeper parts balanced with good tracks. Taking parts 1 and 2 together, this walk adds up to an SE500: 500m of ascent over about 13 miles, burning off an average of 2100 calories.
Well behaved dogs are welcome on this walk. You can follow the
route
on OS Maps.

Title: Autumnal Weekend On The Slopes Of Skiddaw
Summary:
At 470m above sea level, Skiddaw House is the highest hostel in Britain. It was built around 1829 as a 'Keeper's lodge' and grouse shooting base for George Wyndham, the third Earl of Egremont. The building was originally divided into two separate dwellings; one side for the gamekeeper and his family and the other for a shepherd's family. The Earl and his shooting parties also had a few rooms to stay in when they came to visit. In 1986 the two dwellings were converted into the hostel it is today.
Skiddaw House operated as a youth hostel from 1987 until 2002, when it closed and began to fall into disrepair again. But with the help of the previous hostel manager, many volunteers and the Skiddaw House Foundation, the hostel was renovated and reopened in 2007. The building retains many original features, which combined with its interesting history and remote location make the hostel a unique place to stay.
One of the great features of Skiddaw House is its remote location, offering stunning views of the surrounding Lakeland fells. This venue is an OutdoorLads favourite and is truly special, right from the moment you park up you'll understand why this is so glorious!
However, the remote nature of the hostel means it is lacking the mod cons we may be used to, such as heating. Don't panic, there are a number of open fires throughout the building which helps keep it warm, but the bedrooms do not have any heating. Full bedding of 15tog duvets and pillow are provided but some may prefer to pack their own sleeping bag. Boots are also not allowed to be worn inside so we recommend packing slippers too!
Itinerary
Friday Afternoon/Evening -
Arrive at the car park for 15:00, meet the rest of the group and we will hike up to the hostel together,
sharing the load of weekend food supply bags
. Please have your head torch handy in case we start to lose the light! Once we have arrived and found our beds and settled in a bit, we'll have a briefing and dish out the traditional OutdoorLads buffet.
Important: If you're not able to arrive at the car park for 15:00, please message the event Leader at least a week before the event and we'll see what we can do. The walk in from the car park is over an hour long. Depending who signs up, we may be able to organise a second walk-in to the hostel with prior notice. There's no phone signal at the parking location or the venue. I'll share a route map from car park to hostel prior to the event in case of emergency.
Saturday Day -
A simple cold breakfast will be available. The main activity of the day will be a bit of a Wainwright epic, as we tick off up to 5 "Wainwrights," with the main attraction being Skiddaw (931m) on our hike. I expect we'll cover 14km in no more than 7 hours, with a total ascent of 1000m. However, if we're moving a bit slower or there is appetite to cut the walk short, we will be able to cut out some sections.
Saturday Evening -
Pop your feet up and unwind from the day's walk. We'll have a hearty evening meal to warm us back up, followed by some games and good laughs. While the hostel has a few, if you have a favourite travel size board/card game why not bring it?
Sunday -
Breakfast is provided once more then we'll all band together to tidy and clean up the hostel to how we found it (takes no time at all with so many) before we need to vacate by 11am. Once done we will take everything we brought back to the car park and then people might want to head home, or into Keswick for an afternoon touristing. I'll aim to lead a quick nip up to Blencathra (868m) via Hall's Fell Ridge, and back down to the car park. This is around 8km, 700m ascent, and should take around 4 hours.
Other information
Dogs:
The event leader very much welcomes well behaved, quiet dogs on this event. They should be able to cope with and enjoy a long mountain walk, be friendly with other dogs and people in a fairly small hostel, not go upstairs whilst wet, and be exceptionally well behaved around food. The venue has capped the number of dogs at three, and they and their humans will be assigned to one room, leaving other bedrooms available for humans only. Contact
support@outdoorlads.com
to reserve a dog space.
Food:
Please note that all food/drink provided will be plant-based. Whilst I encourage you all to embrace plant-based foods for the weekend, you are welcome to bring whatever buffet contributions you like. You'll also need to bring a packed lunch.
Skiddaw House requires a 1 hour hike to access it from the car park. To ensure everyone arrives safely we ask that all attendees meet at the car park for 3pm Friday so that we can hike up together. You will need to carry everything you need for the weekend including food and drink, plus a modest bag of supplies from the event leader in one trip - so pack light!

Title: Hamble and Warsash: Ferry, Foreshore and a Freshwater Finish
Summary:
We'll set out from the waterside village of Bursledon, where modern suburbs jostle old cottages and boatyards. We'll glimpse the river's transformation from backwater to playground for yachts, with marinas and moorings filling its lower reaches. Following the river south to Hamble-le-Rice, we'll take the pink ferry to Warsash - jaunty, yachty settlements both - and we'll soon arrive at a sweeping shingle shore on The Solent, where we'll pause for lunch with great views. Turning inland we'll follow the causeway along the river's eastern shore to either conclude our walk directly back to Bursledon, downing a cool pint, or indirectly at Andark Lake in Swanwick, plunging into the cool waters.
The sights:
Bursledon:
A picturesque River Hamble village with a strong maritime heritage. Its shipbuilding industry flourished in the C18 and C19, producing wooden vessels from local yards. Surviving boatyards, cottages and former workers’ buildings reflect this past. The village’s wooded creeks and scattered historic buildings create an attractive waterside setting, though later housing has altered its traditional character. Boomers and Generation Xers may recall the popular series BBC series
Howard's Way
(1985-1990) which was filmed all across the places we'll see, but centred on Bursledon and the Elephant Shipyard and Jolly Sailor pub.
Hamble-le-Rice:
A historic riverside village shaped by farming, boatbuilding and sailing. St Andrew's Church, Hamble-le-Rice dates mainly from the C12 and retains medieval features. The village grew as a maritime centre, with C18 and C19 boatbuilding followed by modern yachting. Its narrow lanes, cottages and busy waterfront combine historic charm with a lively nautical atmosphere. Its maritime importance expanded during WWII when its river and foreshore became part of the D-Day preparations. Air Service Training repaired thousands of Spitfires here, while the harbour serviced landing craft and naval vessels. The village also played a role in the secret PLUTO fuel pipeline project, which supplied Allied forces after the Normandy landings
Warsash:
A former fishing and ferry village on the River Hamble, with origins in salt production, fishing and boatbuilding. Maritime activity expanded during the C19, and the waterfront retains attractive cottages, pubs and former marine buildings. Later development has increased its size, but its coastal setting, village lanes and views across Southampton Water preserve a distinctive maritime character. Warsash was also a major WWII naval training centre, with HMS
Tormentor
based on the Hamble preparing landing craft crews for amphibious operations, including D-Day. Troops and vessels gathered for the Normandy landings
The ferry:
You will need to bring £3 in cash to pay for the ferry crossing.
Swimming at Andark Lake:
This is entirely optional. Andark Lake is a purpose-built inland diving lake at Swanwick, near the A27. The lake offers confined openwater conditions with good onsite facilities, including changing rooms with showers, free WiFi, a café and shop. We'll get around 45 minutes to an hour to swim and a session is £7.95. The water is currently 26 degrees Celsius, and there is beach entry to the water. If you'd like to swim, click
here
and select 16.00. Booking in advance is advisable in case the weather is warm.
The
route
(please click the link to go to the Ordnance Survey website)
:
We'll walk through Bursledon village west along Kew Lane and a little of Hungerford before taking a bridleway south to cross Hamble disused airfield. We'll emerge from this on Satchell Lane and walk south down Hamble High Street to The Quay where we'll catch the ferry. Disembarking form this, we'll walk along Shore Road and Strawberry Field, following The Solent Way to the sea. At Cowes Lane we'll head inland, and follow Hook Park Road and Newtown Road north back to Warsash. At Passage Lane, we'll head back towards the river and follow the coastal path and the causeway to Swanwick. We'll then have a choice: either go down Oslands Lane to Andark Lake, or follow Bridge Road (the A27) over the River Hamble and heading south down Church lane and Station Hill back to Bursledon Station, a route that those who swim will also follow.
Dogs:
I love having dogs on the walks I lead, and this walk is very suitable for them although there are some country lanes and suburban streets to walk along and roads to cross. A dog off its lead must be under control.

Title: Cheddar Gorge, Velvet Bottom, Beacon Batch and Rowberrow
Summary:
This is a 17km circular route, starting in Cheddar, and walking up the western edge of Cheddar gorge, located within the Mendip Hills National Landscape.  The walk commences with the toughest ascent of the day, and passes the lookout tower and pulpit rock, where you can get far reaching views right across the Somerset levels towards the Quantock hills in the distance, as well as cliff top views down into the gorge itself. From here we descend down to the flower rich limestone grassland of the Black Rock and Velvet Bottom Nature reserves.  We then ascend up to the Beacon Batch trig point, which at 325 metres, is the highest point within the Mendip Hills, where weather permitting,  we should get spectacular views across North Somerset and the Bristol channel, before dropping down to the woodland of Rowberrow Warren, and from there returning to the start point in Cheddar.
This walk is approximately 17km in length, has some very steep sections, with a total height gain of 460 metres.

Title: Wargrave, Hurley & the Dew Drop: Boys, Boots, Boats & Beer
Summary:
Please note that the
capacity for this event will initially be set at 15,
but I may look to expand to 20-25 as we look to promote this one at Reading Pride for potential new members in the region. If capacity is reached please add yourself to the waitlist and I will revisit after Reading Pride on 5th Sept.
Overview:
Lace up your boots for a 12.3 mile adventure that showcases some of the best of the mid Berkshire countryside. Starting in the upmarket riverside village of Wargrave, we'll meander through peaceful fields of wheat and sheep, shaded woodland and quiet country paths before dropping downhill and joining the Thames Path for a beautiful stretch alongside the river. As we reach the halfway point, we'll arrive in the historic village of Hurley where we will stop for a lunch break.
Refuelled and ready, we'll leave the river and Hurley behind and head back uphill into rolling farmland and extensive woodland. After a couple of miles with the worst of the climbing out of the way, out of the blue we will reach the Dew Drop Inn, a hidden gem tucked away in the woods and the perfect excuse for an afternoon drink (hydration is important, after all!).
From the Dew Drop we have the final four-mile stroll back to Wargrave, including one more long but gradual climb, where tired feet, rosy cheeks and plenty of laughs will mark the end of the day packed with riverside views, woodland trails, good company and and iconic pub stop. 🍺🥾🌳
The Route:
Starting from Wargrave Station, we will initially walk through the old part of the village, past the church and cross the High Street. We will then proceed through Upper Wargrave, with it's more modern housing estates, before getting to the village boundary and open countryside.
Initially we walk through fields and then an extensive section through woodland (Bottom Boles Wood), taking the Chilterns Way/Berkshire extension for some of the way. After climbing up into the small hamlet of Warren Row, we then take a long, straight and gradually downhill route down the valley towards the Thames, and after crossing a main road we take a lane to eventually join the Thames Path.
We then walk east along the Thames Path for about 1.25 miles until we get to Hurley, where we will stop for lunch. There are benches by the river and also in the village centre. After lunch we will continue to walk North through the village, crossing the main road again, and then it's initially an uphill section back out of the Thames Valley through fields and woodland.
When we get to the scenic Ashley Hill forest we will have a pub stop at the iconic Dew Drop Inn, and afterwards will continue through the forest. We continue through sections of fields and woodland until we get to another extensive area of woodland and will take the wide Knowl Hill bridleway along a gradual but long uphill section to the top of Bowsey Hill. From the top we continue through more woodland and at the fringes eventually re-join the route that we took out of Wargrave where we will retrace our steps back to and through the village.
The route can be found
here
:
The Sights:
Wargrave:
is a Thames-side village in Berkshire, nestled where the River Thames meets the River Loddon. Dating back to Saxon times, the village features a several historic buildings centred around its attractive High Street and the 13th-century St Mary's Church, with parts of the church reflecting centuries of architectural development. The village is also home to the Grade II-listed Wargrave War Memorial, designed by the distinguished architect Sir Edwin Lutyens and unveiled in 1922.
Hurley:
is one of Berkshire's most historic Thames-side villages, with origins dating back to Saxon times. The village is best known for the remains of Hurley Priory, founded in 1086 as a Benedictine monastery, parts of which survive within the present-day St Mary the Virgin Church, Hurley. Adjacent to the priory stands The Olde Bell, established in 1135 as the monastery's guesthouse and widely regarded as one of England's oldest continuously operating inns. The village also has strong links to the Glorious Revolution, with nearby Ladye Place serving as a secret meeting place for those who supported the accession of William III.
The Dew Drop Inn:
is nestled in the heart of Ashley Hill Forest and often described as a "little pub in the woods". It's a Grade II-listed country pub that has welcomed travellers and locals since the 18th century. Built in the mid-1700s from traditional flint, chalk and red brick, the inn retains many original features, including exposed beams, open fireplaces and its intimate woodland character. Historically, it served as an important stopping place for forestry workers, horse riders and travellers crossing the surrounding countryside.
Ashley Hill Forest:
is an expanse of ancient woodland, once part of the historic woodlands that covered much of the Chiltern foothills. The forest combines ancient broadleaf woodland with areas of conifer plantation that are now being carefully restored to their natural character, and is popular with walkers, cyclists and horse riders. A notable landmark is its impressive Giant Sequoia, believed to be one of the tallest trees in Berkshire.
Dogs:
Well-behaved dogs are welcome, there will be a few areas where we are walking along or crossing roads but the majority of the walk is in open countryside where dogs can be let off the lead. Please abide by the Countryside Code (
https://tinyurl.com/rlqvp3h
) and remember not everyone loves dogs as much as you do so be mindful of other members.

Title: Jack and Jill went Up the Hill, the Lads Likewise to See Her
Summary:
Jack and Jill, in case you are wondering, are a pair of windmills on the Downs behind Brighton, he a brick tower mill, she a wooden post mill. Jack is currently indisposed: he's lost his sails and dome while restoration work goes on, but Jill has just been fully restored and now opens on Sundays in August and September, hence this walk. Even if you've seen the windmills lots of times before, seeing inside Jill, seeing the Grade I-listed Elizabethan mansion that is Danny House, seeing the views of the Weald to the north and Brighton to the south, seeing the fare in the tearooms of Ditchling and seeing your OutdoorLads mates should be enough reasons to venture up the hill again.
The sights:
Danny House:
A Grade I-listed Elizabethan mansion at the foot of Wolstonbury Hill, built in 1593–95 by George Goring on the site of an earlier medieval house. Designed in the shape of the letter 'E' in honour of Queen Elizabeth I, it is an outstanding example of Elizabethan architecture, with a monumental red-brick east front and an elegant Georgian south façade added in the 1720s. During the First World War, Prime Minister David Lloyd George lived at Danny House, where meetings of the Imperial War Cabinet were held. On 13 October 1918, ministers agreed the armistice terms to be offered to Germany, a decision that helped bring the war to an end. The surrounding parkland retains ancient trees, including the celebrated "Danny Old One" oak (perhaps the oldest oak tree in the Sussex Weald with a girth of 9.9 metres), and historic woodland.
Wolstonbury Hill:
A 58.9-hectare biological Site of Special Scientific Interest. Rising to 206 metres, it extends northwards into the Weald off the South Downs, offering extensive views across both the South Downs and the Weald. Notable landmarks visible from the summit include the Clayton Windmills, Ditchling Beacon, Devil's Dyke and Chanctonbury Ring. The hill is owned and managed by the National Trust, and part of it is designated as a Scheduled Monument.
Jack and Jill Windmills:
Jill is a beautifully restored wooden post mill dating from 1821, moved from Brighton in 1850 and open to visitors on the day of our walk. Nearby Jack, a brick tower mill built in 1866, remains structurally intact but is currently without its cap and sails while restoration work continues. Admission to Jill is free, with donations welcomed, and refreshments are usually available. For more information, click
here
.
Ditchling:
Built on a crossroads which has the C13 St Margaret's Church high above it, it is very pretty in flint, timber, brick and tile. Interesting buildings include: 'Anne of Cleves' House', which was given by Henry VIII to his fourth queen as part of her marriage annulment settlement; and 'Sopers', the home of wood engraver, stone sculptor, type designer and sexual abuser Eric Gill, which became an artistic community and inspired a museum of the arts and crafts. This was designed in 2014 by Adam Richards Architects. Noted Ditchling residents include Raymond Briggs, Donald Sinden and Dame Vera Lynn. Ditchling also has a good supply of pubs and tearooms of which we'll make use. Just outside Ditchling at Keymer is another windmill, Oldland Windmill, a wooden post mill from 1703, restored and functioning.
The
route
(please click the link to see it at the Ordnance Survey)
:
We'll follow the B2166, walking on the pavement west out of Hassocks, before turning south down New Way Lane before quickly taking a footpath to Danny House along its avenue. We'll get back on to New Way Lane before turning west along a bridleway and then south up Wolstonbury Hill. Descending the hill we'll turn east towards Rockrose. Emerging on to the the A273 we'll head south using its pavement to pick up the South Downs Way to Clayton Windmills, have lunch, then head further east and then north to descend the Downs along the Sussex Border Path. We'll then reach Ditchling for tea and cake. Leaving the village by heading northwest along Lodge Hill Lane, we'll pass Oldland Windmill and reach Mill Lane. Ockley Lane will take us back into Hassocks and Grand Avenue back to the station.
Dogs:
I love having dogs on my walks and this walk is very suitable for them unless it's really hot. There will be some stiles and livestock, plus some roads to walk along. A dog off the lead must be obedient.

Title: Autumn retreat to The Gower
Summary:
Join Ben for a quiet and relaxed weekend on The Gower Peninsular.
This early autumn weekend is the perfect chance to get some fresh sea air in peaceful countryside.  OutdoorLads hostels are a great way to quickly meet new friends and find out about what we do. Attending your first hostel event could be a daunting experience if you don’t know what’s going to happen so why not have a read of our '
My First Hostel Event
' guide.
Kilvrough Manor is hidden away in its own wooded grounds in the South of the Gower making for a warm and comfortable retreat as Autumn sets in.  With three rooms to socialise in along with a fire pit area there's plenty of space to play board games or chat away and make new friends aswell as catching up with old ones over the weekend.  Please note that the hostel has a no nut policy.
Friday evening:
Arrive, settle in and meet with fellow ODLers.  A simple evening meal (included in the event cost) will be provided followed by a welcome meeting.  The rest of the evening is yours to enjoy.
Saturday:
After breakfast (included in the event cost) we'll head out for a 10 mile walk taking in views of Pobble Bay. You will need a relatively good level of fitness for the walk.
Please bring a packed lunch
and maybe a flask of hot drink if it's cold.
If you don't fancy coming on the walk, you can choose to stay in the hostel or explore nearby Oxwich Bay, Port Eynon or Rhossili.
Saturday evening:
Relax and socialise or help out preparing the 2 course evening meal (included in the event cost) which we'll all enjoy.
Sunday
After breakfast we'll help clean and tidy away leaving the hostel as we found it.  After that you can explore The Gower before heading home.

Title: Secret Oxford
Summary:
Pub fights, prostitution, mummification and afternoon tea.
A 5 hour  stroll back through Oxford's past looking at some of the people, places and stories you wished they'd taught you in history lessons. We'll discover the birthplace of two of England;s most famous kings, see the oldest continually serving coffee house in Europe, find the alley where prostitutes plied their trade in the 13th century, spot the site of the pub where 63 students were killed in a pub brawl.
Newbies to the city will adore our next port of call, Magdalen College, considered by many to be Oxford's most beautiful college.
Founded in 1458 by William of Waynflete, and granted by Henry VI
It's imposing tower completed in 1509 contains 10 bells, the heaviest was cast in 1623 and weighs 17cwt. Charles I, who was based in Oxford during the English Civil War, watched the 1st Siege of Oxford from the top of Magdalen Tower. In a tradition dating back to Henry VII the College choir still sings from the top of it at 6am on May Morning.
The Cloister was constructed between 1474 and 1480, as was the Grade 1 listed chapel.
For the past 300 years a herd of fallow deer has grazed in The Grove which is where the royalists kept their ordnance during the civil war.
We will 'do' the tree-lined Addison's Walk - a one mile walk through meadow land bounded on 3 sides by the River Cherwell. From here we will see the terrace which houses Oscar Wilde's old rooms.
Alumni include: Edward Prince of Wales (later Edward VIII and Duke of Windsor), John Betjeman, Cardinal Wolsey, Jeremy Hunt, John Redwood, Earl Spencer (DIana's brother), Andrew Lloyd Webber, Seamus Heaney and CS Lewis - who would meet JRR Tolkien in his rooms here.
LGBT links: Oscar Wilde and his lover Lord Alfred Douglas were both students at Magdalen as was the author Alan Hollinghurst. Lord John Wolfenden, whose landmark Wolfenden Report, famously recommended the decriminalisation of homosexuality was a don here.
We will stop for a cup of tea etc at the Old Kitchen Bar with its terrace overlooking the punters gliding past on the River Cherwell below.
Finally we will explore the highlights of the Ashmolean Museum to see a Lesbian bank note, Guy Fawkes's lamp, a jewel belonging to Alfred the Great, a mantle owned by Pocohantas's Dad, the ornate carved Indian doors that Lawrence of Arabia erected next to his swimming pool and say hello to 'Djed the Dead', the mummy of an 8th century BC Egyptian prophet who is not resting in peace.
NB THIS EVENTS IS NOT SUITABLE FOR DOGS AS THEY ARE ARE NOT ALLOWED INTO THE ASHMOLEAN DUE TO PRICELESS ARTEFACTS NOR INTO MAGDALEN COLLEGE AS THEY SPOOK THE DEER IN THE PARK THERE.
Difficulty & Distance: 5 mile (approx) flat walk on city pavements throughout,

Title: For Halloween: Gothic Ruins, Graveyards and Ghost Trains
Summary:
Six hours or so hours after the witching hour (which is apparently between 3 and 4 in the morning) we'll start our walk. Our route to reach some Halloween hallmarks (castles, graveyards, relics) will proceed along trackways (or, if very muddy, quiet tarmac lanes) and go to West Grinstead, home to some vintage railway infrastructure, and Knepp Park, home to Tamworth pigs, longhorn cattle and Exmoor ponies. If the countryside all around looks like a tidy, landscaped park, then the park itself looks increasingly unkempt as the livestock graze and biodiversity increases. All in all, urbanity in the smart houses, rusticity in the remote farms, fantasy in the old remains, felicity in the autumn colours.
The sights:
Christ's Hospital:
An independent school founded for poor boys by Edward VI in 1553, but moved from the City of London to Sussex in the C19. Around 900 girls and boys (whose education is still paid for by bursaries) who wear Tudor-style uniforms of dark blue serge with yellow stockings. Main buildings are huge and in a simplified Gothic-Elizabethan style by Aston Webb, begun 1893, finished 1902.
West Grinstead:
The topographer Ian Nairn is worth quoting: 'Halfway between Horsham and the Downs, at a point where the Weald has opened out and become more park-like, with trim hedges rather than copses. The Burrells with their pair of Nash houses [Knepp Castle and West Grinstead Park] and attendant landscaping have given it a character unlike anywhere else in Sussex: The Weald has been at first tamed, then let back, on a leash as it were, to be wild within limits.' Gateland's Farm is C17, Grade II-listed, gabled, tiled and timber-framed but with an alarmingly leaning chimney. St George's Church is by the River Adur and has stone slab roofs and a low, shingled spire. Early Norman north aisle, the rest is C13 but with a C15 timber porch. Good monuments such as brasses and busts by Rysbrack and Flaxman. Glebe Cottage is C18 and Glebe House is c1600. West Grinstead Station was on the Beeching-cut Horsham-Shoreham line and retains platforms, signage, signals and a British Railways Mark 1 carriage in green Southern livery.
Knepp Estate:
Old Knepp Castle is a fragment of an C11 century Norman keep, 10m tall, with a mound and a small motte. New Knepp Castle was built by John Nash in 1809. Stucco, not stone, and in a flamboyant and irregular design. Burnt in 1904 and rebuilt exactly. Park by Humphrey Repton. The website states about the estate:
'
3,500 acres in the heart of the Sussex Weald. Knepp Estate...has been owned by the Burrells for over 220 years...Until recently most of the land was devoted to traditional arable and dairy farming but in 2001 we shifted our focus entirely and embarked on a series of regeneration and restoration projects aimed at nature conservation - or 'rewilding', as it has come to be known. We are still farming, just in a less intensive way - producing organic, pasture-fed meat from free-roaming herds of animals within the Wildland project.' We'll mostly just see the parkland.
Dragon's Green:
A hamlet of pretty weatherboarded and timber-framed cottages but also some 1950s houses which give a suburban feel. The George and Dragon Pub is very pleasant. Handsome Newbuildings Place is 'Artisan Mannerist' in style, dated 1683, stone and brick built with a Dutch gable and home to Wilfred Scawen Blunt, author, poet, traveller and breeder of Arab horses, who is buried in the grounds.
Dogs:
I love having dogs on my walks and this walk is suitable for them. It is of moderate length, but there will be fields with livestock and a number of stiles and roads to negotiate. A dog must be obedient if it is off the lead.
The
route
(please click the link in red to see it and note that if the autumn has been very wet, much of the route will be switched to tarmac lanes):
Setting off in a southerly then southeasterly direction we'll take the Downs Link former railway line and cycle path to Southwater and eventually to West Grinstead Station. Heading southwest along Park Lane we'll reach West Grinstead hamlet where we'll cross the River Adur and then, heading east, the A24. Routes through the Knepp Estate will enable us to pick up a bridleway will take us north past Green Street to the lane to Dragon's Green. A route west than northwest, then north along a lane will head back past Netherwood and Lawson's Farm to the cycle path which will return us, via the outward-bound route, back to the station.

Title: 1066 Country: East we'll Ease through Woods and Weald
Summary:
We’ll start in the mellow gold light and bonfire-scented air of a mid-October morning. We'll join the 1066 Country Walk trail through gentle fields and the Great Wood, a sprawling remnant of the ancient Wealden forest. We'll see towering oak and sweet chestnut standing in a blaze of copper and amber, their leaves carpeting the paths. We'll imagine the historical upheaval that was the Battle of Hastings, almost 960 years ago to the day. We'll admire a little of Battle Abbey, founded by King William in 1070 to celebrate his victory (and perhaps atone for his savagery). We'll take lunch and a pint in the village of Westfield and perhaps further refreshment back in Battle at the end.
The sights:
Battle Abbey:
Founded by William I in 1070 to give thanks for his victory. Remodelled in the C13. Standing in partial ruin, its gatehouse intact and dominating the town centre. Cloister arches, monastic remains, and views over the slope where Harold’s army fell bring the Conquest vividly to mind. It was destroyed in 1538 by a tyrannical beneficiary of the central, powerful English state that William created: Henry VIII. The abbey is managed by English Heritage and costs £17 to enter, so we won't be doing that.
The Battle of Hastings:
This paroxysm will have occurred almost 960 years ago on the day of the walk, when on 14 October 1066, William, Duke of Normandy, defeated King Harold II in a brutal clash that lasted most of the day and led to the loss of 6000 lives. Whether Harold's army had walked 250 miles from Stamford Bridge near York over 12 days, or whether they had sailed down the east coast, the Saxon army fought with astonishing resolve. Fighting with spears, swords and axes, they advantageously held the high ground and held the Normans off behind a shield wall. The tide turned when Harold momentarily lost control of his army when, sensing victory at the misapprehension that the Duke of Normandy was dead, they surged down the hill, abandoning the high ground and their shield wall. The Duke threw back his helmet to show that he still lived, his army rallied, and their archers and cavalry - the latter not encountered by Saxon armies before - massacred them. Legend says that Harold fell with an arrow in the eye, a fate depicted on the Bayeux Tapestry. Legend also says that his body was so vengefully mutilated that only his wife, Edith Swan-Neck, could identify it by way of secret marks on it known only to her. The consequences of the defeat were far-reaching: Norman overlords replaced local Anglo-Saxon rulers; feudalism and hierarchy were introduced; governance, culture, architecture and justice were reshaped; nascent women's rights were overturned; and England was orientated away from Scandinavia in the direction of the European core.
Westfield:
A village with its roots in the Domesday Book but not much else of historical interest. St John’s Church, rebuilt in 1815 on medieval foundations, stands at the heart of the village, its churchyard flanked by venerable yews. We will pause here for lunch and a pint at the New Inn.
The
route
(click the link to see the route)
:
We'll head down Station Approach to Lower Lake, then head northwest along Upper Lake into the town of Battle. A short excursion down Park Lane will allow us to see a little of the battlefield and abbey without having to pay £17. Returning to the High Street, we'll walk northwest up to Mount Lane before turning off and following a footpath past Little Park Farm to Marley Lane. Footpaths will take us northeast to Sedlescombe, then, having crossed the B2244, further footpaths will take us to east to Cottage Lane which will take us into Westfield for lunch at the church and a pint. We will then veer west and follow the 1066 Country Walk all the way back to Battle and the railway station.
Dogs:
I love having dogs on the walks I lead and this should be a great dog walk with woods and fields for them to run free, although the latter may contain livestock, and there will also be some country lanes and pavements. A dog off the lead must be obedient.

Title: NOTTINGHAM Indoor Climbing (Basford) – Beginners welcome
Summary:
Join OutdoorLads at Nottingham Climbing Centre
Climbing evenings are held regularly and we tend to go to the local pub – The Lion for refreshments and a social gathering afterwards where they have a wide variety of beverages both alcoholic and non-alcoholic.
NOTE: If you are climbing with us for the first time
, either as an experienced climber or beginner, please send a note to the
Event Leader
telling them about your experience and goals. There is a limit to the number of beginners that we can accommodate at each session. Each beginner needs to be supervised so we need to ensure there are enough experienced climbers to help you out. Climbing is great fun! It's a fab workout, in a social environment, and anyone can do it! Give it a go!
Nottingham Climbing Centre
Nottingham Climbing Centre is equipped with walls and routes to suit all skill levels and groups of climbers, whether you are a novice looking to try climbing for the first time, or an experienced lead climber, you’ll find an area to challenge you. With 28 Top Ropes routes available as well as 24 Lines of Lead climbing for the more advanced individuals. In addition, 6 auto-belays are available, so there is always the opportunity to climb, even if the numbers don’t match up. The available bouldering walls also provide that extra physical and mental challenge for those looking for something slightly different from rope work. Both Bouldering and Rope Climbing routes range from 4a – 8a.
I'm new to Climbing - can I come along?
If you've never climbed before or need a refresher, the leader will sign you into the climbing centre as a
supervised climber
so that you can come and give it a try (it can be helpful to message the leader to let them know). If you enjoy your climbing experience, and would like to come climbing more regularly, we will also happily show you the ropes and teach you everything you need to know to climb safely.
Do I need to be Supervised as a Climber?
If you answer
NO
to any of the following three questions, then you will need to arrange to be supervised. If you can answer YES to all these questions, you can sign up to this event as normal:
Can you fit a climbing harness correctly?
Can you tie yourself to the end of a rope using the correct knots?
Can you belay another climber correctly and confidently?
To come along, you will need to register via this event page and to climb you will need to pay an entry fee directly to the climbing centre when you arrive, please see their
website
for up-to-date prices. We ask that all members sign up through the event page to make sure the event leader has all information of the members attending.
To climb at Nottingham Climbing Centre you will need to:
-     Complete a climbing waiver for the centre (please arrive early to do this the first time, or better still complete it online before you arrive)
-     Pay the Lifetime Registration Fee - £6.00
-     Pay an Entry Fee directly to the climbing centre - £9.50 (ensure you mention ODL)
-     Hire shoes (if you don’t have your own) - £3.50*

Title: Nottingham Bouldering (Lenton) - MONDAY - Beginners Welcome
Summary:
Swap trainers for climbing shoes and join OutdoorLads for an evening of INDOOR BOULDERING at Nottingham’s newest bouldering venue
NOTE: If you are climbing with us for the first time
, either as an experienced climber or beginner, please send a note to the
Event Leader
telling them about your experience and goals. There is a limit to the number of beginners that we can accommodate at each session. Each beginner needs to be supervised so we need to ensure there are enough experienced climbers to help you out. Climbing is great fun! It's a fab workout, in a social environment, and anyone can do it! Give it a go!
What is Bouldering?
It's a form of climbing where instead of long high routes, the 'problems' tend to be shorter and focus on technique, balance, body positioning and sometimes power. Because of this different emphasis, bouldering doesn't have the hassle of climbing with ropes, harnesses and belaying, which makes it an excellent activity for newcomers to the sport. No wonder it's often regarded as the 'purest' form of climbing.
If you're a seasoned climber you won't need convincing about the benefits of bouldering, but for those who've never climbed more than a staircase, the benefits are wide ranging: from the physical - improved strength, tone, balance, power and coordination; mental - problem solving, focus, concentration and body awareness; to the emotional - relaxation, a sense of achievement and a feeling that mind and body are working together perfectly ('feeling psyched'). On top of all this, bouldering tends to be a very social sport where you can hang out with mates and each have a go as you feel regardless of what level you climb at.
I'm new to Bouldering - can I come along?
If you have never tried bouldering before it is recommended that you have a guided session from the event leader, who will go through everything you will need to know to boulder safely before joining in with the rest of the group.
I've been Bouldering before?
As above, everyone attending the event  must abide by the centre's T&Cs etc. As an experienced boulderer you are responsible for your own safety, actions and involvement at all times. As such, you should use your own judgement in taking up advice given either by OutdoorLads Volunteers or other experienced climbers.

Please ensure you only sign up for this event if you

Never climbed before? Need a refresher on the basics? Answered NO to any of the three questions above? You will need to

If you are subsequently unable to attend, please cancel off the event as 'no-shows' are not only rude, but also frustrating for the leader & other attendees who may have travelled over an hour away to climb with you!
Redpoint Birmingham Climbing Centre
Indoor climbing centres offer the challenges of climbing that you'll find on natural rock crags - simply indoors! It's a fun way to stay fit, make new friends & develop your climbing skills.
Climbing
- Unlike Indoor Bouldering there is a certain amount of skill to be mastered, such as tying in knots & belaying a partner, as well as the climbs being higher than in bouldering. If you are new to climbing or would like a refresher, then this is just for you!! If you’ve climbed before, can safely tie into a harness & can competently belay, then there’s plenty of choices of top-rope & lead climbing on offer here.

The bouldering rooms are just as interesting as its climbing routes, over 200 bouldering problems have been organised into graded circuits to provide something for everyone.

Title: Lochnagar
Summary:
Lochnagar
, the crown jewel of the Cairngorms is a prominent Munro rising 1,156m in the Cairngorms National Park, famous for its dramatic northern corrie and the dark lochan nestled at its base.  The 19km circuit begins at the Spittal of Glen Muick, following a well-maintained path through heather before climbing steeply up the ladder to the plateau to reach the true summit,
Cac Càrn Beag
, which offers panoramic views.  The route takes roughly 6 to 7 hours to complete, combining rich literary history, that drove a young Lord Byron to immortalise these very cliffs in verse over two centuries ago.
Why not make a weekend of your trip to Braemar, with a nearby

walk on the Saturday too!

Title: Quiet Cotswolds: Tysoe, Epwell & Winderton
Summary:
The Cotswolds are justifiably protected as one of England's
Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty
. But that label brings with it a huge volume of visitors - especially to places like
Stow-on-the-Wold
,
Bourton-on-the-Water
and
Chipping Campden
.
Fortunately, there's a quieter side to the Cotswolds which has the same beautiful landscape but far fewer tourists. This two-county walk will explore some of those hidden gems!
Starting from
Middle Tysoe
, we head across the fields and soon face a sharp climb up
Old Lodge Hill
into a beautiful wooded area. As we emerge from the trees, we cross over the border from Warwickshire into Oxfordshire.
At
Shenington
, we join a stretch of the
Macmillan Way
- a long-distance route devised to raise funds for Macmillan Cancer Support - which runs from Lincolnshire all the way down to Dorset. We'll walk through some classic Cotswold scenery as we head down to the charming village of
Epwell
and our lunch stop.
Suitably refreshed, we’ll cross back over the border into Warwickshire and enjoy some spectacular views on the approach to the small village of
Winderton
with its prominent hilltop Victorian church.
The final leg of our walk gives a distant view of
Compton Wynyates
- a Grade I listed Tudor country house which is still in private ownership, undisturbed (and inaccessible) by visitors.
Another sharp climb takes us up to the highlight of our walk -
Tysoe Windmill
and stunning views across the surrounding countryside. Built in the early 18th century, the mill operated until 1915 when it was struck by lightning! Today, it sports a magnificent set of recently restored sails.
Dogs are welcome:
There are some short stretches on country roads and village streets. We may encounter sheep, lambs, cows or horses and there are a few fields where landowner signs request dogs on a lead.

Title: Laying bare the past in Haslingden Grane
Summary:
Our
7 miles (10.9KM)
walk explores the Grane Valley, once home to over 1000 people and part of the Forest of Rossendale, a medieval hunting forest until 1587.
Many settlements and houses have long since vanished, but we will encounter many derelict remains of homes that originally populated the area in the 16th century.
Calf Hey Reservoir, built in the 1850s robbed struggling communities of the best land for farming and the final straw was in the 1880's, with drastic falls in commodity prices.
People abandoned their homes in the poorer uplands across the region, but the depopulation of the Grane Valley is one of the most stark instances, and the upland area we will explore as a part of todays walk.
Our highest point will be Hog Low Pike at 383m, providing panoramic views across the Ribble and Bowland Valleys, Pendle Hill and the Yorkshire Dales beyond.
We will have the option of a well earned drink at the Grey Mare pub after the walk.
The rough upland footpaths and open moorland mean that sturdy boots are really an essential for this walk and being steady underfoot across open moorland and on rough paths.

Title: ODL goes to Canada and Respects to a British Icon
Summary:
In a first for OutdoorLads, we're going to Canada! But worry not! No expensive flights, no jet lag and no passports needed, as this Canada is a little hamlet in the New Forest!
Our
route
takes us straight out on to Canada Common, where the Forest's iconic ponies, donkeys and cattle roam free. After crossing the A36, we'll pass along the streets of West Wellow and then on to quiet lanes and footpaths to the smaller neighbouring hamlet of East Wellow.
Here we will find St Margaret's Church which is the final resting place of Florence Nightingale. The church itself dates back to 1215 and has many interesting wall paintings inside depicting figures such as St Christopher, Thomas Becket and St Margaret of Antioch after whom the church is named.
Florence Nightingale is generally regarded to be the founder of modern nursing, putting an emphasis on compassion, commitment to patient care and diligent and thoughtful hospital administration that had not previously been seen. She came to prominence during the Crimean War in the 1850s, and earned the nickname "The Lady with the Lamp" due to her routine of making ward rounds of the wounded soldiers at night.
With such a legacy, an offer was made for her to be buried at Westminster Abbey, but her family declined, chosing instead for her to be buried in the family plot alongside her parents. The family lived at nearby Embley Park. While the tombstone itself is reasonably large, there is no grand memorial, simply bearing her initials and birth and death dates.
With respects duly paid, we'll move on through a mix of lanes and paths following the River Blackwater upstream. After crossing back over the A36, we'll take a break at the lovely Cuckoo Inn in Hamptworth.
Our route on from there will pass through the hamlet of Nomansland with its pretty village green, through some mature oak woodland and then back on to the open spaces of Canada Common where we started.

Title: Reflections of Summer - Mid Afternoon Walk
Summary:
Join Andy and OutdoorLads for a stunning
Saturday afternoon
stroll around Moses Gate Country Park !
Starting at Moses Gate Country Park, the route begins in a diverse natural landscape made up of woodlands, wetlands, and open meadows. The park, also known locally as Crompton Lodges, is rich in wildlife, with several lodges (small lakes) that attract birds such as herons, ducks, and kingfishers. Well-maintained paths and peaceful surroundings make it an ideal starting point, offering a calm introduction before the journey unfolds.
From here, we join the historic Manchester, Bolton & Bury Canal, a largely restored waterway that provides a scenic and tranquil corridor through the landscape. Following the towpath, (along the Kingfisher Trail), we pass through Nob End, a designated Site of Special Scientific Interest. For those who have attended previously, we will get a chance to see how the canal reservations are progressing now that the bridge is now re-opened.
This area is particularly notable for its unusual plant life, shaped by the region’s industrial past, as well as its striking views over the River Irwell and surrounding countryside.
Bolton’s largest nature reserve
At 750 acres this is Bolton’s largest nature reserve. Home to mill lodges, woodland and plenty of heritage, wildlife meets industry in a peaceful site where there is always something to see.
This area is an
SSSI
(
Site of Special Scientific Interest)
. It’s a conservation designation used in the UK to protect areas that are important for their wildlife, plants, geology, or landforms.
In simple terms, it means the area is considered
nationally important
for science and nature.
What makes a place an SSSI?
A site might be designated as an SSSI because it has:
Rare or endangered plants or animals
Unique habitats (like wetlands, heathlands, or ancient woodlands)
Important geological features (rocks, fossils, land formations)
For example, Nob End is an SSSI because of its unusual plant life, which developed due to the area’s industrial past.
Why are SSSIs protected?
SSSIs are legally protected to:
Prevent damage from development or pollution
Manage land in a way that supports wildlife
Preserve them for research, education, and future generations
Can people visit them?
Yes—many SSSIs are open to the public, and you can walk through them. However, visitors are usually expected to:
Stick to paths
Avoid disturbing wildlife
Not remove plants, rocks, or other natural features
So when you pass through an SSSI on your route, you’re walking through an area that’s considered one of the UK’s most valuable natural environments
This walk is mainly flat - approximately 4 miles.

Title: A Literary Loop around Haworth Moor
Summary:
This scenic 8‑mile circular walk begins in
Haworth
, the historic moorland village famed for its steep cobbled Main Street and its deep connection to the Brontë family. With the Parsonage Museum nearby and sweeping views toward the Pennines, Haworth provides an evocative starting point for a day immersed in Yorkshire’s literary landscape.
Leaving the village, the route heads out toward
Penistone Hill Country Park
, a broad expanse of former quarry land now reclaimed by heather, grasses, and wildlife. Its rolling terrain and wide horizons offer early panoramic views across the moors, setting the tone for the rugged scenery ahead.
From Penistone Hill, the path continues westward toward the quiet valley of South Dean Beck, arriving at
Brontë Bridge
, a picturesque stone crossing set in a sheltered hollow. The sound of the beck and the surrounding moorland create a timeless atmosphere, echoing the landscapes that inspired the Brontë sisters.
Beyond the bridge, the route climbs steadily onto the high moor, following well‑trodden tracks toward
Top Withins
. The ruined farmhouse sits isolated on the ridge, long associated romantically if not literally with the Earnshaw home in
Wuthering Heights
. The approach is dramatic, with sweeping views and the unmistakable sense of wildness that defines this part of the Pennines.
The return leg descends from Top Withins toward the moorland village of
Stanbury
, offering a change of scenery as the rugged heights give way to lanes, cottages, and valley views. Here we can enjoy a well‑earned refreshment stop at the
Wuthering Heights pub
, a welcoming spot with views across the surrounding hills.
The final stretch follows paths and tracks that gradually lead back towards Haworth and brings us once again into the village.

Summary:
Join Samuel for a 7 mile/11.2km circular walk from Coombe Abbey Country Park. In 1771 the 6th Baron Craven commissioned Capability Brown to modernise the landscape around the former Cistercian monastery at Coombe Abbey. Brown swept away the elaborate Elizabethan gardens and landscaped the park to create a serpentine lake, sweeping views and extensive new planting.
We will start by weaving through the wooded paths of the park before exiting onto bridle paths and country roads, skirting Birchley Wood before returning to Coombe Abbey via the Twelve O'clock ride.
Due to the nature of the ground. I recommend walking boots or shoes for this walk due to the uneven ground in parts.
